Making gives learners a public object through which knowledge can be applied, tested, discussed and improved, and three conditions without which it does not work.

t: Technology is a means, not the learning outcome
d: A practical test for whether a piece of technology belongs in a lesson, and why the answer is often no.
Why artifacts, talk-throughs and reflection give a stronger picture than attendance, and what each one uniquely catches.
Three parts, all required, and why the number of levels in a subject is derived rather than chosen.
Age is a proxy for readiness. The proxy was removed and readiness measured directly: what that changed, and what it cost.

t: A makerspace is not a computer lab
d: Where almost all connectivity is mobile, the missing thing is not a signal. It is a bench, a machine, and somebody who knows how to use them.

t: Why the music room is next to the electronics bench
d: Multidisciplinary work is part of the definition of a makerspace, and it does three specific jobs.
A card nobody buys is design feedback that cost an afternoon, and five ways this goes wrong.

t: What counts as a solved local problem
d: Three tests, why a technically excellent build can fail all of them, and why a definition this strict makes the goal harder on purpose.

t: Measuring what cannot yet be claimed
d: The evidence that makerspaces improve livelihoods does not exist. What an organisation should do about that.
The case for sustained school-age engagement, without turning age into an entry rule for maker education.

t: Why an Ecosystem Builder Has to Teach
d: Why DreamSpace Academy runs education itself: it is where the people who build and sustain an innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem come from.
The Maker Journey, Definition of Done, pedagogy axes and delivery lessons that make up DreamSpace Academy's teaching method.
A definitional review of Challenge-Based Learning — its lineage, its framework, and the single feature that distinguishes it from project- and problem-based learning.

A definitional review of the term entrepreneur — the fifteen elements that recur across two centuries of definitions, the six a leading review distils from them, and why the field declines to settle on one.
A definitional review of "changemaker" — a movement term coined at Ashoka rather than an academic construct, deliberately ungated by design, and therefore uncountable.

A definitional review of cognitive apprenticeship — the premise that trade apprenticeship makes process visible while schooling leaves thinking invisible, the six teaching methods and four design dimensions that follow from it, and what the evidence base does and does not support.
A definitional review of Papert's constructionism — what it adds to Piaget's constructivism, why its author refused to define it, and whether maker education actually implements it.
A definitional review of co-creation across four traditions that use the word differently, and the feature that separates it from consultation, participation and collaboration.

A definitional review of the entrepreneurial ecosystem — a concept that reached policy ubiquity in under a decade while its own leading proponents were describing it as tautological, under-theorised and long on component lists but short on causal mechanism.

A definitional review of experiential learning — Kolb's synthesis of Dewey, Lewin and Piaget, the four-stage cycle and its two dialectics, and why the cycle and the Learning Style Inventory rest on entirely different evidence.

A definitional review of entrepreneurship education — the about/for/through distinction, the intention-as-proxy problem, and an evidence base whose effects are small, dosage-dependent, and occasionally negative.

A definitional review of communities of practice — the concept's origin as an analytic of how learning happens in practice, its later reinvention as a prescriptive management tool, and the critiques of power and harmony that follow from both.

A definitional review of grassroots innovation — the two research strands that developed the term independently, the social-economy criterion that distinguishes it from market innovation, and the unresolved question of whether an aided innovation still counts.

A definitional review of what to call a mission-driven trading organisation — and the finding that "impact venture" has no sector standard, only one institutional definition, which places it by financing stage rather than by values.

A definitional review of how learning in maker settings is assessed — process versus product evidence, portfolios, self- and peer-assessment, rubrics and their limits, and the interview method for eliciting what a learner understands about an artifact they built.

A definitional review of unstructured, self-directed making time as a distinct pedagogical mode — the names it goes by, the benefits claimed for it, the well-documented equity critique, and the finding that open and structured modes are complementary.

A definitional review of the makerspace — why the term resists definition, what actually separates a makerspace from a hackerspace, a FabLab, a TechShop and a community workshop, and how thin the outcome evidence still is.

A definitional review of innovation — a term with no authoritative definition, a literature that says so openly, and the one distinction every source nonetheless agrees on, namely that an idea becomes an innovation only when it is adopted and used.

A definitional review of Problem-Based Learning — the medical-education pedagogy in which an ill-structured problem starts the learning, and the reason it shares an acronym with a pedagogy it is not a variant of.

A definitional review of the organisational lifecycle — a descriptive family of stage models whose biological metaphor imports assumptions about ageing, decline and irreversibility that the empirical evidence does not support.
A definitional review of Project-Based Learning — the five criteria that screen a project in, the progressive-era lineage, and the acronym it shares with an unrelated pedagogy from medical education.
A definitional review of maker education — its lineage, what the systematic reviews actually report as outcomes, and the persistent gap between its learning claims and its evidence.
A definitional review of social enterprise — a term with four competing definitions, no settled boundary, and a legal-form question that is separate from it in every jurisdiction.

A definitional review separating Direct Instruction — a specific family of scripted, field-tested curricula — from direct and explicit instruction as a general teacher-led mode, and reporting the unsettled dispute over how much guidance a novice learner needs.

A definitional review of social franchising — replication of a proven social model through a franchise-like agreement, the spectrum it sits on, and the quality-control-versus-local-adaptation tension that is the field's central unresolved problem.
A definitional review of the term startup — why the literature has settled on no single definition, and which variables actually do the discriminating work.

A definitional review of "underserved" — a relational claim about inadequate provision of a named service, distinct from marginalised, vulnerable and disadvantaged, and contested for locating deficit in the community rather than in the systems that failed it.

t: Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET)
d: A definitional review of Technical and Vocational Education and Training — the term, its rival names, the formal/informal split, the record of dual-system transfer, and an evidence base whose measured employment effects are far smaller and less durable than the policy rhetoric implies.

A definitional review of tinkering — the Exploratorium tradition, its constructionist lineage, what "low floor, wide walls, high ceiling" actually specifies, and why the literature does not show that tinkering alone produces conceptual learning.

t: Pitch day, one year of growth, grit and guts
d: Seven young entrepreneurs pitched what they had built after a year in the campus. The clearest twelve-month follow-through in the record.
The second run of the campus first photographed in August 2024, and the start of the year that ended in a pitch day.
The four-stage scale describing what a learner’s making is for, Explorer, Maker, Innovator, Changemaker. It runs across every subject rather than inside any one of them.
One of the four positions on the Maker Journey. A stage answers the question what is this work for, and entry to each is condition-based rather than scheduled.
The first stage, “What can I do?” Encountering tools, materials, ideas and peers through low-pressure experiences. Open entry: a person walks in.
The second stage, “Can I make something?” Focused practice that builds dependable capability in a chosen subject, through assessed projects.
The third stage, “Can I make it better?” Applied inquiry: using capability from one or more subjects to investigate a real problem and test alternatives.
The fourth stage, “Can I make a difference?” Entered by producing a grassroots innovation, not by time served, enthusiasm, or finishing a programme.
Someone who has entered the venture pathway on demonstrated intent and commitment, but has not yet produced a grassroots innovation. A candidate becomes a Changemaker by producing one.
Depth within one subject, attached to a programme. A level is three things at once (a descriptor, a volume of notional learning hours, and an assessable artifact) and all three are required.
The number of levels in a subject, derived from the genuine capability thresholds between a beginner and independent practice, never chosen to match another subject or fill a column.
Depth, Independence, Complexity, Impact, the four ways in which one level is genuinely deeper than the level below it.
A block of work inside a single programme, for example “Level 1, Unit 2 of 4”. Units organise delivery; they do not carry a certificate of their own.
The thing a learner enrols in and is certified for: one subject, one level, with published prerequisites, learning outcomes, units and assessed work.

A coherent area of learning and practice through which someone can build capability. The published list names the domains currently offered or in development; it is not a permanently closed set, and domains may be added, combined or retired.

A physical area of the building, its equipment, the capability held there and the people who gather around it (electromechanics, software, media, music. Facilitated on rotation and not owned by one person) a deliberate rule, because capability that belongs to an individual leaves when they do.
A learner’s record of depth across subjects (say, robotics at level 4, music at level 1, plus stage milestones) held together rather than averaged.
A recorded, never-graded checkpoint inside the Innovator and Changemaker stages, a field test completed, a user trial run, a community agreement reached.
A programme’s entry assessment: direct evidence that a learner holds the prerequisites, however and wherever those were acquired.
Someone who stops before the end of a stage or programme. Leavers and their destinations are recorded as carefully as completers.

The person running a session or a floor. A function held on rotation rather than a permanent post, and the role the wider field also names, the shift is from lecturer to facilitator, mentor and collaborator.
The job splits three ways rather than one: the organiser sets the challenge and its context, the teacher is accountable for the content, and the coach works with the learner on their own work.
A paired, longer-term relationship attached to a person rather than to a place, the usual delivery form for venture-pathway support.
Structured, syllabus-following teaching, tuned to the maker model. One of the two delivery modes, and a first-class one rather than a fallback.

Unstructured, self-directed, peer-driven time on the floor. It is not assessed by default, a learner may later submit something made here as programme evidence if it meets the criteria, and it is timetabled deliberately rather than left over.
The Maker-stage frame: a scaffolded brief supplied by the facilitator, with the solution left to the learner. Narrow in method, open in outcome.
Sustained work on a driving question producing an artifact, the Innovator-stage default, and the only thing the abbreviation PBL means on this site.
Starting from a real situation rather than a syllabus, and running Engage → Investigate → Act. It spans the Innovator and Changemaker stages; the Changemaker stage adds real stakes to the Act phase.

Open, playful investigation of materials, led by curiosity rather than a set task. The Explorer-stage default, and guided throughout: the facilitator keeps it safe and helps when asked, without turning it into an exercise.
The standard adjective for how this education is delivered, hands-on workshop, hands-on learning, hands-on experience.
An Explorer-stage entry format giving access to tools, ideas and possible domains. Unassessed, and no prior capability required; places, safeguarding and practical conditions still apply.
An intensive cohort format, running anywhere from a few days to six months, most often around three. It has a start, an end, and a funnel.
A one-off, typically one day, with a prepared agenda.
One meeting inside a programme, bootcamp or school term, the unit that carries a shape: opener, taught content, practical work, reflection.

Seymour Papert’s learning theory: knowledge is built rather than transmitted, and it is built most readily when the learner is consciously making a public entity, something that can be shown, discussed and argued with.
Learning through a cycle of concrete experience, reflection, conceptualisation and active experimentation. It is where the requirement for a written reflection at certification comes from.
Making expert thinking visible: the facilitator models the reasoning aloud, coaches while the learner attempts it, and withdraws support as competence grows.
Education organised around making things, the field this system belongs to. Cross-disciplinary by definition, and framed around a mindset rather than a set of machines.
A distinct tradition, originating in medical education, in which an ill-structured problem is the starting point and the curriculum follows from it.
Technical and vocational education and training, the sector a reader will most likely file this work under, and the closest formal comparator to what happens here.
The completion standard: six evidence states that assessed work must show, in any order, Aim, Options, Made, Evaluated, Shared, Refined.
Evidence state: what the learner was trying to do, and for whom. It may have been settled at the start or discovered halfway through.
Evidence state: that more than one way of doing it was considered, and that a choice between them was made for a reason.
Evidence state: something exists. An artifact, a recording, a performance, a working system.
Evidence state: it was tested against the aim, by some means the learner can describe, measurement, a listener, a user, a run that failed.
Evidence state: it left the bench. Shown, performed, published, handed to someone, or taught to another learner.
Evidence state: something changed as a result of the evaluation or the sharing, including a documented decision to change nothing, and why.
The made thing itself, object, recording, software, performance or documented service. The first of the three sources of certificate evidence.
A structured oral explanation of the work at assessment: how it works, why it was built that way, and what was tried and rejected.
A short written or recorded account of the process, the third source of certificate evidence, and the step that makes an experience transferable to the next problem.
The hard result is the artifact. The soft results are the capabilities it evidences, persistence, judgement, collaboration, the ability to debug.
What a completed programme produces. It requires the artifact, the talk-through and the reflection (three sources, not one) and it names the programme and level, never a stage.
Work to which the Definition of Done applies, from the Maker stage upward, which is exactly where certification applies.
The community makerspace and digital-education hub this education runs in, one space that moves people from making, to innovation, to enterprise. Written in full on first mention.
The generic sector term: a shared physical facility with tools, materials, expertise and a community around them, open to people who could not assemble any of that individually.
The keyword of the model: the surrounding conditions (tools, examples, expertise, introductions, first customers, peers) that make entrepreneurial and innovative activity possible.
A group whose shared work is how its members learn. Newcomers begin at the edge on real tasks and move inward, which is a description of a functioning makerspace floor.
Several domains under one roof. Real problems are not single-subject, people arrive through different doors, and capability transfers sideways between domains.
Science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics, the frame this organisation uses across its programmes.
One replicated makerspace site, specified to open below one million rupees, the smallest configuration that can still deliver the standard.
A replication model in which independent local operators run the model under a shared standard, support package and identity, with social outcome rather than profit as the return.
What must stay the same across every site for a certificate to keep its meaning, the completion standard, the stage definitions, the safety rules and the assessment method.
The pooled library of tested projects, briefs, curricula and assessment materials that every site draws from and contributes back to.
The four things the MakerSpace offers a person. They run as threads inside every stage; they are not a sequence and they are not the four stages under another name.

Income and work, read across three tiers of very different evidential strength. Tier 1: small income, a maker selling what they made. Tier 2: a sustained livelihood, by venture or by wage. Tier 3: work created for others, when a venture employs, contracts or buys locally.
Research and development, entrepreneurship, and business and financial literacy, woven through every domain and every stage rather than appended as a final module.
The first area of the strand, make it work. Systematic inquiry applied to something real: prototype, test, document, repeat.
The second area of the strand, make it matter. Turning a working solution into something someone wants: opportunity discovery, value proposition, a minimum viable product, and a pitch.
The third area of the strand, make it last. Costing, pricing, bookkeeping, marketing and operations.
Make something, price it, sell it to a stranger, and work out afterwards what the result told you. The cheapest way to put a maker in front of a real user.
A solution to a real problem. It may be technical, academic, personal or commercial, and it belongs to the Innovator stage.
An innovation rooted in a real community challenge, passing three tests, all of them: the problem came from the community; a user outside the space has tested it; and someone depends on the outcome.
The route from a person with intent to a venture that stands on its own: three stages, one thread and four support modes.
Stage one of the venture pathway: entry. Two routes in, discovered, where field workers find someone already doing something; or co-created, where a learner arrives through the Maker Journey.
Stage three of the venture pathway: turning a grassroots innovation into something that can keep running, a venture, a service, or a practice that a community sustains.
What is offered at and after the gate: co-creation, bridging, domain expertise, and funding. Available in any combination and any order.
Connecting a local problem to a non-local resource, and the resource back to the problem, introductions to funders, specialists, networks and international opportunities.
A venture that came out of a real community challenge, has a credible path to paying for itself by trading, and cannot yet do so without support. All three clauses are required.
The point at which a venture pays for itself by trading and no longer needs support. The event has a name; the graduated thing is simply a self-sustaining venture, or a business.
The general term for any new venture seeking a viable model, whatever its legal form: for-profit, non-profit, cooperative or collective.
The person who starts and runs a venture. Entrepreneurs are what an ecosystem is made of, and support is not conditional on having come through the academy’s own programmes.
Structured support for an early venture (space, mentoring, introductions, and sometimes capital) for a defined period with a defined end.
The life stages of an organisation itself, idea, start-up, growth, maturity, and what follows. A descriptive frame used to place an organisation, not a pathway anyone is put through.
The organisation this reference belongs to: a non-profit social enterprise working on local socio-economic challenges, founded on 30 September 2018 in Batticaloa, Sri Lanka.
The futures that become imaginable for a community when its people, knowledge, culture and opportunity meet through co-creation. Emergent, collectively held, and never a fixed list.
The frame for people who came through the academy’s programmes and now staff or run them, and the name of one documented route out of the learning journey.

What follows the learning journey: an open set of destinations rather than a fixed list. Documented routes include building a venture, research and academia, activism and community leadership, employment and freelancing, and growing an existing family enterprise.
Work on the conditions that let a divided community function, cohesion, information integrity, inclusion and trust. Here it is a lens across all three pillars, not a fourth pillar beside them.

A named making domain with its own area, equipment, craft and artifact. A lab is named only when it holds four things at once: the making domain, a named maintainer, a team, and a date the statement is true as of.
A DreamSpace site outside the founding location. That is the only sense in which the word is used here.
Whoever delivers a bootcamp, workshop or school session, including people the academy does not employ.
The person accountable for a lab. The title follows the accountability and moves when it does.
A residential or multi-day intensive, run to a fixed start and end date.
The written account of how the work is supposed to produce the result, inputs, activities, outputs, short-term outcomes, medium-term outcomes and impact, with the conditions each step depends on.
Education, Innovation, Entrepreneurship, the three domains everything the organisation runs sits under. This site covers the first and the third in full, and the second where the two meet.
What this organisation calls itself, a non-profit social enterprise, meaning it trades and reinvests rather than distributing a surplus.

Everything a person needs to solve a problem themselves and to keep solving the next one, skill, tools, a network, capital, permission to act, a problem worth solving, and standing enough to be heard. The whole bundle, not the first item.
A relation, not a location: local to wherever this work is being done. Reading it as one fixed place makes the purpose untrue the moment the model crosses a boundary.
Who a piece of work is rooted in, and who bears its outcome. Scoped per project rather than defined once, and made operational by the first and third grassroots-innovation tests.
Inadequate or absent provision of a named service, relative to need. Incomplete until two blanks are filled in: underserved in what, relative to whom, so every project states its axis.
The method: building with a community rather than for it, from problem definition through to who owns the result. It is also one of the four support modes.
Co-learn, co-innovate, co-produce, what happens between people in the ecosystem. An open set, not a closed taxonomy.
The countable unit behind the goal of one hundred by 2050: a grassroots innovation for which all three tests hold. Rung four of the innovation ladder, and nothing below it.
The global goals adopted in 2015. Results are mapped to them so that outcomes can be read against a shared frame.
Six levels that are never interchangeable: inputs, activities, outputs, short-term outcomes, medium-term outcomes, long-term impacts.
Four rungs that are routinely reported as one: 1 a learner project, 2 a functioning prototype, 3 tested by an external user, 4 a grassroots innovation.
How many people an activity touched. An output, not an outcome, and reported as such.
Capability measured at the start and the end of a programme, tied to that programme’s own curriculum.
Contact at 3, 6, 12, 24 and 36 months after leaving, against a livelihood baseline taken at intake. It is what makes the “Earn” question answerable at all.
A claim this model is testing rather than asserting, labelled as such wherever it appears, most importantly the second tier of “Earn”.
A figure supplied by the person or organisation it describes. Recorded and labelled, never presented as a verified count.
What a result cannot show, sample, method, timing, attribution. Published alongside the result, not in a footnote after it.

A non-profit social enterprise that co-creates an ecosystem to tackle local socio-economic and environmental challenges through education, innovation and entrepreneurship. It was founded in Batticaloa, Sri Lanka, in September 2018.

t: Is “social enterprise” a claim that you do not rely on grants?
d: No — and it is not an admission of dependence on them either. The phrase describes a structure, not a funding position. The work has been funded by grants and partnerships, by revenue earned through services and trading, and by the founders’ own capital. The relative shares have never been measured, so no ranking between them is claimed in either direction.

t: Where does education fit in the wider model?
d: It is one of three pillars, alongside innovation and entrepreneurship, and it is the front of the whole system: it is how capability gets built before anything else can happen with it. The MakerSpace is the place that building happens in.

t: How many labs and ventures do you have?
d: Neither number is published. A lab is named only when it has a making domain, a named maintainer, a team and a date the statement is true as of; a venture count would need a stated role and a stated population it is counted from. Until those conditions are met, a figure would be misleading.

t: What part of your model is not proven?
d: Whether this particular rural pathway produces durable income. That entrepreneurship contributes to economic development is well evidenced; whether this maker-to-venture route does the same, and at what rate, is a hypothesis, and is why the measurement work exists.

t: Which Sustainable Development Goals do you claim?
d: Nine, each with something specific carrying it. Two came off the list recently, one removed because the evidence did not fit the goal’s own definition, and one held as stated intent because the outcome has never been measured. Both reasons are published.

t: What is MakerSpace by DreamSpace Academy?
d: It is a community makerspace and the learning system that runs inside it. People learn by making things, working on projects and real local challenges, explaining and reflecting on their work, and taking on more of it independently over time.

t: Is it a school, a training centre, or a makerspace?
d: It borrows from all three and is none of them exactly. It is not a conventional classroom and not a computer lab. It is a space with tools, materials and people, in which learners explore interests, build real capability and work on problems that exist outside the building.

t: How is this different from a normal classroom?
d: Learners do not mainly listen and repeat. They make things, test whether they work, explain the decisions behind them, improve them, work with other people, and apply what they know to projects and challenges that have not been solved for them in advance.

Learning by designing, building, testing, repairing and explaining tangible work. Technology is one possible tool in that, never the point of it, a well-made piece of furniture, a recorded song and a working sensor all qualify.

It depends on the programme, the places available, safeguarding requirements and any stated prerequisites. Open Explorer experiences need no prior skill at all; structured programmes use a placement check.

t: Is there a minimum or maximum age?
d: Placement is based on demonstrated capability, not age, age is not used as an entry rule, a band or a label anywhere in the system. Safeguarding and legal duty of care still apply, and an individual programme may have practical participation requirements.

t: Does a learner need good school grades?
d: Usually not. What matters is what a learner can already do and what support they need. Where a structured programme has genuine prerequisites, a placement check tests for those directly rather than using school results as a proxy for them.

t: How do you decide which level a learner starts at?
d: A placement check looks at demonstrated knowledge, skill and independence. Prior learning counts however it was acquired (at school, at work, online, or from a relative who repairs things) and it does not need a certificate behind it.

The domains currently documented are maker education and fabrication, digital education, AI programmes, AI with electronics, software and tech-entrepreneurship, creative arts, and fitness and sport. This is the current portfolio rather than a fixed structure: domains may be added, combined or retired. They are not all at the same stage of development, and the site says which is which rather than presenting them as equal.

t: Does everyone have to learn coding or robotics?
d: No. A learner may come in through craft, music, media, art, sport, coding, electronics or another available area, and those practices overlap, with technology supporting work across any of them. The domains sit under one roof deliberately, because real problems are not single-subject and people arrive through different doors.

t: What are Explorer, Maker, Innovator and Changemaker?
d: The four stages of the journey, describing what the work is for. Explorer is open discovery; Maker builds dependable skill in a chosen subject; Innovator aims that skill at a real problem; Changemaker is reached by producing work that came from a community, has been tested by someone outside the space, and that someone depends on.

t: Is everyone expected to become a Changemaker?
d: No. The stages describe possible routes, not a ladder everyone must climb. Leaving with a real skill, a finished project or a job is a complete outcome, and every stage records its leavers and where they went, rather than counting only the people who stayed.

A level belongs to a programme, inside the Maker stage. It is three things at once, a description of capability, an expected volume of learning, and an assessable piece of work. It is never a label attached to a person: there is no such thing as “a Level 3 learner”.

t: How long does the journey take?
d: There is no single duration, and none is published. It depends on the programme, what a learner already brings, the projects they choose and the evidence they produce. Progress is based on demonstrated capability, not on time enrolled.

From the Maker stage onward, work is judged against a published Definition of Done, six evidence states that must all be present, in any order. Certification additionally requires three things: the artifact, a talk-through of it, and a written reflection. Explorer work is deliberately unassessed.

The emphasis is on demonstrated work rather than a written exam or a single mark. A learner shows what they made, explains how it works and why they made the decisions they did, and says what they would change.
It names the programme and level completed and the evidence used to judge it. It represents demonstrated work against a published standard, not attendance, which is why the standard is published.

t: Are the certificates nationally or internationally accredited?
d: Not as a system, and this is genuinely unsettled. Unless a particular programme names an accrediting body, a certificate should be understood as issued by DreamSpace Academy itself.

Facilitators, whose job changes as a learner becomes more capable: they teach directly, demonstrate safe practice, coach, ask questions, and connect people to others who know more. Guidance is highest where knowledge is lowest, structured teaching is a first-class part of this, not a fallback.

t: How are learners kept safe around tools and equipment?
d: Every programme publishes its tool, material and safety requirements, and access to equipment is matched to demonstrated readiness and supervision. Safety is a design constraint on what a programme may offer, not a poster on a wall.

t: What happens when a learner struggles, or something fails?
d: Failure is information, and it is treated that way, as long as safety holds. A facilitator can add instruction, demonstration, practice, feedback or peer support, and work can be revised before it is assessed. One of the six evidence states is literally Refined.

t: Will this help a learner get a job or start a business?
d: It builds practical, digital, creative, innovation and enterprise capability, and enterprise runs through the whole journey rather than being added at the end. Small income is a realistic near-term outcome. A sustained livelihood is something the academy measures rather than claims, nobody is promised a job, a business or an income.

t: How do you choose which community problems to work on?
d: The problem has to come from the community, not from a competition brief or a funder’s theme. Learners investigate the situation with the people affected, test whether the response is useful to someone outside the space, and a prototype on a bench is never counted as a solved problem.

t: How can a donor or partner tell whether this works?
d: Activities, outputs, outcomes and long-term impact are reported separately, on their own lines, so that each can be read for what it is. Limitations are published alongside results, and documented curriculum, actual delivery and independently verified evidence are treated as three different claims.

t: What is this model’s biggest limitation?
d: There is no strong causal evidence that makerspaces improve long-term livelihoods in settings like this one, not in the academy’s own record, and not in the literature reviewed for this site. The system is built to generate that evidence rather than to assume it, and the instruments for doing so are published.

t: How do I find out what is running now, and where?
d: This site describes the system rather than the current timetable, because programmes, locations and dates change. For what is open now (including places, dates, language of delivery, any fees or funded places, and accessibility arrangements) contact DreamSpace Academy at info@dreamspace.academy or through dreamspace.academy.

t: What should I ask before enrolling?
d: Useful questions: which programme and level, what it costs and whether funded places exist, where and when it runs and in which language, what the placement check involves, what tools and materials are provided, what the safeguarding and supervision arrangements are, and what a learner leaves with. A programme that cannot answer these is not ready to be offered, and every one of them is part of the published programme specification.

t: Is there support for learners with a disability, or who need another language?
d: Accessibility and language needs are handled per programme rather than by a blanket policy, and they are part of what a programme has to state before it is offered. Raise the specific need when you enquire. It is a practical question about the room, the tools and the facilitator, and it is better answered before enrolment than after.

t: How can a parent, school, donor or community organisation get involved?
d: By asking what is running now, visiting where that is appropriate, proposing a school or community partnership, contributing expertise, equipment or materials, or funding access and delivery. The route for all of these is info@dreamspace.academy.

t: Can this model be run somewhere else?
d: That is the intention, as a social franchise rather than a set of unrelated spaces sharing a name. What must stay identical is the completion standard, the stage definitions, the safety rules and the assessment method; the domains, language, timetable and problems worked on are deliberately local.
